ocar.opportunity: Animals mix innate and learned values of cues when they choose to approach or avoid. A synaptic map of how mushroom-body (learned) and lateral-horn (innate) pathways meet would show how experience can override instinct.
ocar.challenge: Innate and learned valences are thought to be computed in distinct brain areas, but the circuit mechanisms that integrate them, and by which learned valences can override innate ones, are poorly understood.
ocar.action: Eschbach, Fushiki, and colleagues in eLife (2021) use electron microscopy in Drosophila larva to map all neurons downstream of all mushroom-body output neurons and their interactions with lateral-horn neurons, then test functional connectivity and behavior for selected convergence cells.
ocar.resolution: They identify 62 neurons per hemisphere as direct MB–LH convergence points, including a subtype of 10 that receive excitatory input from positive-valence MB and LH pathways and inhibitory input from negative-valence MB pathways. Two of these encode integrated odor value and bidirectionally regulate turning; for one, aversive learning skews inputs toward inhibition.
ocar.future_work: The authors speculate that learning could skew excitation–inhibition onto these neurons and thereby modulate turning; broader tests of remaining convergence subtypes and of how learning rewires them are the implied next steps.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly larvae have one brain area for inborn likes and dislikes and another for learned ones. This study maps how those two systems meet, and shows that some meeting-point cells control turning when an odor is attractive.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2021), Eschbach, Fushiki et al. reconstruct larval Drosophila circuits downstream of all mushroom-body output neurons and their contacts with lateral-horn neurons. They report 62 MB–LH convergence neurons per hemisphere and a 10-cell subtype with mixed positive excitation and negative inhibition. Two cells encode integrated odor value, suppress turning when activated, and increase turning when inactivated; aversive learning was verified to shift one cell toward inhibition.
summaries.advanced: Functional and behavioral tests cover two of 10 cells in one subtype, not all 62 convergence neurons. The claim that learning could modulate turning via E/I balance is partly speculative; only one neuron is shown to receive more inhibition after aversive learning. The map is larval, not adult. Optogenetic valence assignment of many MBONs is part of the study but is not a whole-brain connectome.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly larvae have one brain area for inborn likes and dislikes and another for learned ones. This study maps how those two systems meet, and shows that some meeting-point cells control turning when an odor is attractive.

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM reconstructions now produce terabyte- and petabyte-scale wiring diagrams, so the community needs a way to judge whether a connectome product is accurate enough to reuse without redoing years of proofreading.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation, anisotropic alignment, and synapse classification all inject merge and split errors. Exhaustive human proofreading does not scale: MICrONS visual cortex and the Janelia Hemibrain already required many staff years. Graph reconstructions are becoming too large for exhaustive checking.
ocar.action: Bishop, Matelsky, Wilt, Downs, Rivlin, Plaza, Wester, and Gray-Roncal present CONFIRMS at EMBC (2021): a scalable toolkit that marries human-in-the-loop inquiry with large-scale graph analysis for black-box quality assessment, illustrated on a recent reference dataset. Forced-choice tasks support focused rather than exhaustive proofreading.
ocar.resolution: The toolkit is released to assess reconstruction quality via targeted inquiry and network-based measures, with source code at github.com/aplbrain/. The authors argue this workflow can characterize large connectomes more quickly for reuse.
ocar.future_work: They note that as graphs grow, exhaustive proofreading may become infeasible; future evaluators should keep pairing focused human checks with automated graph measures and community adoption of the toolkit.

summaries.beginner: Huge automated brain maps can hide tracing mistakes that ruin the wiring list. This paper offers free software to spot-check a finished map with people and with graph tests, instead of rechecking every cell.
summaries.intermediate: At the 2021 IEEE EMBC, Bishop et al. introduce CONFIRMS for scalable, black-box assessment of nanoscale connectomes. Motivated by staff-year proofreading on MICrONS and Hemibrain, they combine supervised forced-choice inquiry with automated graph analysis on a reference dataset. Code is public; the paper is a methods toolkit rather than a new reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: The reference dataset used for illustration is not named in the selected text. No numeric precision/recall or merge/split rates are reported here. Clinical-relevance language about disease is prospective. Quality measures still depend on some human input; exhaustive proofreading is explicitly treated as increasingly infeasible.

plain_language_summary: Huge automated brain maps can hide tracing mistakes that ruin the wiring list. This paper offers free software to spot-check a finished map with people and with graph tests, instead of rechecking every cell.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain connectomics is becoming feasible for small representative species, which opens a comparative program: recover the archetypal neural architecture of each animal bauplan and detect circuits that converged independently onto a shared layout.
ocar.challenge: It is unknown how each species' connectome differs from close relatives versus whether distant lineages converged on an optimal architecture. Research has concentrated on mouse, fruit fly, C. elegans, and zebrafish, unlike earlier neuroscience that sampled many animals.
ocar.action: Barsotti, Correia, and Cardona review in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021) how molecular, microscopy, storage, and computational advances lower barriers to whole-brain maps, and argue for comparative connectomics across relatively small species spanning the phylogenetic tree.
ocar.resolution: They conclude that comparing maps across representative species can identify fundamental circuit architecture per bauplan and any shared yet nonhomologous circuits from convergent evolution, now that technology makes broader sampling realistic.
ocar.future_work: The review's destination is exploratory comparative mapping across the tree of life, not another single-species flagship volume.

summaries.beginner: Most detailed wiring maps come from a handful of animals. This essay argues we should map more species so we can tell which circuit designs are ancient body-plan features and which evolved more than once.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), Barsotti, Correia, and Cardona survey comparative connectomics. They note conservation of neuroblasts and pallial divisions across deep clades, and that current maps cluster on mouse, fly, nematode, and zebrafish, with additional work in Platynereis and Ciona. They argue small representative species can reveal archetypal bauplan circuits and convergent optima.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/review, not new data. 'Optimal' architecture is a hypothesis to test, not a demonstrated result. Existing-connectome coverage is cited at the level of species lists, not quantitative completeness. Catalog tags are infrastructure; the scientific claim is evolutionary comparison.

plain_language_summary: Most detailed wiring maps come from a handful of animals. This essay argues we should map more species so we can tell which circuit designs are ancient body-plan features and which evolved more than once.

ocar.opportunity: Quantitative 3D ultrastructure of synapses, especially dendritic spines, is the basis for estimating how strongly circuits transmit and for building accurate wiring diagrams. Volume EM now makes long dendritic reconstructions realistic.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy cannot systematically resolve synaptic morphology. Serial-section TEM can, but reconstructing long dendrites by hand is extremely slow. Inhibitory (symmetric) synapses are harder to score than spine synapses because they lack prominent postsynaptic thickenings.
ocar.action: Parajuli and Koike review in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2021) volume-EM studies of three-dimensional synaptic ultrastructure, focusing on rodent dendritic-spine synapses: structural diversity, dendritic organization, presynaptic wiring, and activity-dependent remodeling. They also discuss correlative light-EM, including near-infrared branding as an alternative to immunoperoxidase labeling.
ocar.resolution: Automated EM tools are presented as having addressed low-throughput imaging enough to reconstruct dendritic segments in a realistic time frame. The review compiles principles of spine organization and remodeling from key 3D EM studies.
ocar.future_work: They call for sample-preparation protocols that visualize symmetric inhibitory synapses more clearly and for SEM resolution improvements to support large-scale 3D studies of inhibition.

summaries.beginner: Tiny bumps on brain-cell branches are where many connections sit, but their true 3D shape is only clear in electron-microscope stacks. This review gathers what those 3D pictures have shown about how the bumps are built and how they change with activity.
summaries.intermediate: Parajuli and Koike in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2021) review volume EM of dendritic-spine synapses in rodent brain. They contrast slow serial-section TEM with automated volume EM, cover spine diversity, wiring, and activity-dependent remodeling, and discuss correlative two-photon plus EM, including near-infrared branding. Inhibitory shaft synapses are flagged as under-studied because they are harder to identify.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new reconstruction. Throughput claims are qualitative ('appreciable degree', 'realistic time frame'). Focus is excitatory spine synapses; inhibitory volume-EM evidence is explicitly thinner. Organism is rodent in the review's emphasis, not a named registry volume.

plain_language_summary: Tiny bumps on brain-cell branches are where many connections sit, but their true 3D shape is only clear in electron-microscope stacks. This review gathers what those 3D pictures have shown about how the bumps are built and how they change with activity.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation and synapse prediction now make nanometer-scale neuron reconstructions possible, but large cells still need human proofreading. Focusing that effort on connectivity errors in a single cell's local circuit could finish usable graphs faster.
ocar.challenge: General proofreading inspects large volumes at pixel level and is visually intensive. Automatic segmentation struggles on large neurons. Users also need to understand evolving connectivity graphs, not only to paint voxels.
ocar.action: Gonda, Wang, Beyer, Hadwiger, Lichtman, and Pfister present VICE in Computer Graphics Forum / EuroVis (2021): an analytics framework with automated likely-error detection, synapse clustering, and interactive 3D views aimed at proofreading one cell's local circuit. They evaluate with a user study versus VAST++.
ocar.resolution: Participants found VICE more efficient for proofreading, understanding evolving graphs, and sharing correction strategies, and easier to learn than VAST++ (which required three separate tools). The authors conclude local-circuit proofreading plus automated likely-error detection reduces human effort, especially when many synapses are already known.
ocar.future_work: They release the application and note the approach works best when synapse detections are dense enough for bulk proofreading and automatic classification.

summaries.beginner: Computers that color neurons in electron-microscope stacks still glue or split big cells. This tool points people at likely wiring mistakes around one cell at a time, with 3D views, so they do not have to hunt through the whole volume pixel by pixel.
summaries.intermediate: Gonda et al. in Computer Graphics Forum (EuroVis 2021) introduce VICE for connectivity-focused proofreading of EM segmentations. The workflow uses automated likely-error detection and synapse clustering on a single cell's local circuit, demonstrated on Drosophila brain output circuitry. A user study reported efficiency and learnability advantages over VAST++. Software is at fegonda.github.io/vice.
summaries.advanced: User-study ratings are subjective; quantitative error-rate reductions versus VAST++ are not given in the selected text. The method assumes a high degree of known synapses. Single-cell local circuits reduce clutter but do not by themselves yield a complete volume connectome. Comparison baseline is VAST++, not all contemporary proofreading clients.

plain_language_summary: Computers that color neurons in electron-microscope stacks still glue or split big cells. This tool points people at likely wiring mistakes around one cell at a time, with 3D views, so they do not have to hunt through the whole volume pixel by pixel.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation and synapse prediction make connectivity reconstruction faster than tracing raw pixels, but large neurons still need human correction. Semi-automated 3D merge and split tools could keep reconstruction pace with much larger volumes.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation networks work well in narrow fields of view yet fail on large, complex arbors that need more context. Prior editors (NeuTu, webKnossos) often force scrolling through extensive imagery. Split operations on huge bodies can be slow.
ocar.action: Hubbard, Berg, Zhao, Olbris, Umayam, Maitin-Shepard, Januszewski, Katz, Neace, and Plaza on bioRxiv (2020) introduce Neu3 workflows: affinity-driven merging and cleaving (splitting along supervoxel boundaries), plus focused merging, emphasizing top-down 3D morphology. They measure split processing on 18 bodies from 89 thousand to 90 million voxels.
ocar.resolution: They report average split processing of about 1.4 million voxels per second and argue the tools enabled a connectome on an unpublished dataset of unprecedented scale. Because large false merges are easier to cleave, agglomeration can be tuned toward fewer false splits. Proofreaders often decide from 3D shape alone.
ocar.future_work: Wait times for multi-million-voxel bodies remain; the authors frame further protocol and agglomeration-parameter tuning as the production lesson.

summaries.beginner: After a computer paints neurons in a giant 3D brain picture, people still must glue pieces and cut wrongly joined blobs. This preprint describes a 3D editor that uses the computer's own confidence scores to speed those cuts and joins.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Hubbard et al. present Neu3: 3D visualization plus segmentation-graph operations (merge, cleave, focused merge) driven by affinity scores. Split timing on 18 bodies (89k–90 million voxels) averaged about 1.4 million voxels per second. They report the workflows supported a large unpublished FlyEM-scale connectome and encourage more aggressive agglomeration because large merges are cheaper to undo.
summaries.advanced: The production dataset is unpublished; 'unprecedented scale' is not quantified here. 'Superior performance compared to prior work' is not given as a named metric in the selected extract. Split speed is hardware- and implementation-specific. Catalog method tags include structured-loss affinity segmentation, consistent with affinity-driven edits but not a new affinity net in this paper.

plain_language_summary: After a computer paints neurons in a giant 3D brain picture, people still must glue pieces and cut wrongly joined blobs. This preprint describes a 3D editor that uses the computer's own confidence scores to speed those cuts and joins.

ocar.opportunity: Nanoscale connectomes are graphs too large to search by hand. A readable query language over graph databases would let neuroscientists find motifs and test hypotheses without becoming graph-theory specialists.
ocar.challenge: Converting imagery to graphs shrinks petabytes to megabytes or gigabytes but drops morphology. Even simple neighborhood questions are hard at this scale. Query runtime can explode with graph diameter, limiting how many questions a lab can ask.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Reilly, Johnson, Stiso, Bassett, Wester, and Gray-Roncal introduce DotMotif (bioRxiv 2020; catalog venue Scientific Reports): a neuroscience-oriented grammar over graph databases and analysis libraries for subgraph isomorphism and motif search, demonstrated on simulated graphs and public connectomes.
ocar.resolution: They show motif search on simulated and real public datasets, share example structures, and release DotMotif plus GrandIso and Grand at bossdb.org/tools/. The software is positioned to let scientists query nanoscale networks at scale.
ocar.future_work: Planned work includes automated query-cost validators, a public motif encyclopedia so expensive queries are run once and reused, and faster isomorphism engines.

summaries.beginner: A finished wiring diagram is a huge list of who talks to whom. This software lets scientists ask, in almost plain language, 'find me this little wiring pattern' across those giant lists.
summaries.intermediate: Matelsky et al. (bioRxiv 2020; Scientific Reports in this catalog) present DotMotif, combining graph databases with a neuroscience query grammar for subgraph isomorphism. They demonstrate motif searches on simulated data and public connectomes and release code at bossdb.org/tools/dotmotif (plus GrandIso and Grand). Conversion of EM imagery to graphs is framed as reducing terabytes or petabytes to much smaller networks at the cost of morphology.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal is Scientific Reports while the extracted PDF is the bioRxiv version of the same title. No motif counts or runtime tables appear in the selected extract. Queries remain computationally sensitive to graph diameter. Motif hits are structural, not proof of function.

plain_language_summary: A finished wiring diagram is a huge list of who talks to whom. This software lets scientists ask, in almost plain language, 'find me this little wiring pattern' across those giant lists.

ocar.opportunity: Electron microscopy resolves synapses unambiguously but usually loses the molecular labels that name cell types. A light-microscopy strategy that keeps molecular identity while still scoring putative synapses would let ordinary labs map defined circuits.
ocar.challenge: Synapses span hundreds of nanometers, so diffraction-limited light microscopy is not gold-standard connectivity. Dense tracing needs distinguishable arbors, multiplexed protein markers, and both nano- and microscale views. Small-caliber axons (for example some glutamatergic cells) are harder than the PV axons reconstructed here.
ocar.action: Shen, Harrington, Walker, Cheng, Boyden, and Cai in Nature Communications (2020) combine Brainbow with multi-round immunostaining expansion microscopy (miriEx), a strategy they call spectral connectomics, applied in mammalian brain sections including basolateral amygdala interneurons.
ocar.resolution: They reconstructed morphology and molecular subtype for 53 BLA interneurons in one section; traced 8 postsynaptic PV neurons, 189 innervating PV axons, and 422 PV–PV inhibitory synapses (~40 hours; 422 of about 60,000 inhibitory synapses in the dataset, ~0.7%). Correlative Brainbow plus PSD immunostaining mapped putative inhibitory and excitatory inputs onto aspiny interneurons.
ocar.future_work: They envision routine lab use on other Cre lines and synaptic proteins (transporters, receptors, gap junctions, ion channels); Brainbow titer, expression time, and imaging must be tailored per cell class.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes see connections but often lose the name tags that say which cell type is which. These authors expand tissue and paint cells many colors so a light microscope can both name cells and guess where they touch.
summaries.intermediate: Shen et al. in Nature Communications (2020) introduce spectral connectomics: Brainbow plus miriEx expansion microscopy. In mammalian sections they link 53 BLA interneuron identities to morphology and score putative synapses via synaptic-protein stains. A PV–PV analysis comprises 8 postsynaptic cells, 189 axons, and 422 synapses. Putative synapses required membrane-targeted fluorescent proteins plus pre- and postsynaptic immunostaining.
summaries.advanced: Connections are putative, not EM-verified. The 422 PV–PV synapses are a molecularly targeted subset (~0.7% of inhibitory synapses in that dataset), not a dense connectome. Expansion and Brainbow parameters may not transfer to thinner glutamatergic axons. Catalog method tags include electron microscopy, but this paper is a light-microscopy alternative.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes see connections but often lose the name tags that say which cell type is which. These authors expand tissue and paint cells many colors so a light microscope can both name cells and guess where they touch.

ocar.opportunity: EM, optical microscopy, and X-ray microtomography now generate gigabytes to petabytes of structural brain data. Shared, reproducible pipelines would let labs without local supercomputers still estimate synapse-level graphs or cell distributions.
ocar.challenge: Many neuroscience labs lack compute for this scale. Computer-vision tools are often not portable, and results are hard to reproduce or extend. General workflow engines are built for many small records, not few huge volumetric bricks.
ocar.action: Johnson, Wilt, Rodriguez, Norman-Tenazas, Rivera, Drenkow, Kleissas, LaGrow, Cowley, Downs, Matelsky, Hughes, Reilly, Wester, Dyer, Kording, and Gray-Roncal present in GigaScience (2020) an ecosystem (SABER) of containerized, standardized modules and end-to-end pipelines, with exemplars for EM synapse-level connectomes and X-ray microtomography cell maps, plus large-scale storage and workflow engines.
ocar.resolution: They argue that approaches can be standardized across neuroimaging experiments and applied to diverse datasets. SABER is compared with TOIL, CWL-Airflow, Galaxy, and Air-tasks, emphasizing volumetric blocks, containerized tools, and pipeline optimization.
ocar.future_work: Future work targets usability, GUIs, more reference pipelines, and integration with stores such as bossDB so storage, processing, and visualization share one ecosystem.

summaries.beginner: Brain pictures at synapse scale are so large that many labs cannot even run the analysis software. This paper packages those programs so they can be rerun the same way on big computers, with recipes for electron-microscope wiring maps and X-ray cell counts.
summaries.intermediate: In GigaScience (2020), Johnson et al. describe SABER, a containerized workflow framework for volumetric nanoscale neuroimaging. Exemplars estimate synapse-level connectomes from EM and cell distributions from X-ray microtomography. They position SABER against general scientific workflow managers that lack neuroimaging-specific volumetric deployment and optimization.
summaries.advanced: This is infrastructure, not a new accuracy record on a named EM challenge. 'Accessible' does not include a user-study. Cross-domain applicability outside neuroimaging is asserted, not demonstrated here. bossDB integration is planned rather than completed in the selected discussion.

plain_language_summary: Brain pictures at synapse scale are so large that many labs cannot even run the analysis software. This paper packages those programs so they can be rerun the same way on big computers, with recipes for electron-microscope wiring maps and X-ray cell counts.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome pipelines typically over-segment to avoid catastrophic merges, leaving many split errors for proofreaders. A third stage that uses neuron shape and global context could close remaining splits without creating new merges.
ocar.challenge: Affinity-plus-watershed and region-merging methods decide locally and ignore global consequences. A few merges can fuse several processes, so algorithms favor over-segmentation. Global graph optimization is computationally heavy if applied too early.
ocar.action: Matejek, Haehn, Zhu, Wei, Parag, and Pfister at CVPR (2019) extract a graph from an over-segmentation, prune nodes and edges with morphology-based geometric constraints and two neural nets that learn neuronal shapes, then partition the graph (lifted multicut) instead of greedy merging. They test on four real connectomics datasets.
ocar.resolution: They report an average variation-of-information improvement of 21.3% over input segmentations. Global optimization reduced VI-merge by 15.1% on average versus greedy merging (maximum 23.6% on PNI Test Two). Edge-CNN accuracies are 96.4%, 97.2%, and 93.4% on PNI and Kasthuri sets; recall of true split errors is about 80%.
ocar.future_work: The graph formulation is meant to accept other partitioners and future neuron-type constraints (for example forbidding excitatory–inhibitory merges). Code is pointed at rhoana.org/biologicalgraphs.

summaries.beginner: Computers tracing brain cells often cut one cell into many pieces to avoid gluing two cells together. This method looks at cell shape across the whole volume and decides which pieces to join, using rules inspired by how neurons actually look.
summaries.intermediate: Matejek et al. at CVPR (2019) add a biology-constrained graph-partitioning stage after standard over-segmentation. Geometric filters and two shape-learning nets shrink the graph; lifted multicut then agglomerates with global context. On four datasets they report 21.3% average VI improvement and 15.1% average VI-merge reduction versus a 95%-threshold greedy baseline.
summaries.advanced: VI numbers are dataset-specific (PNI, Kasthuri named in tables). Average 21.3% and per-dataset merge decreases should not be generalized to anisotropic serial-section pipelines not in the test set. Edge-CNN accuracy is not the same as final VI. The third stage assumes a reasonable over-segmentation already exists.

plain_language_summary: Computers tracing brain cells often cut one cell into many pieces to avoid gluing two cells together. This method looks at cell shape across the whole volume and decides which pieces to join, using rules inspired by how neurons actually look.

ocar.opportunity: Isotropic FIB-SEM below 10 nm in x, y, and z traces fine neurites with little alignment burden, but conventional systems are too slow and too unreliable for connectomic volumes. Making FIB-SEM run for years would open large-volume isotropic imaging.
ocar.challenge: Standard FIB-SEM is unreliable beyond a few days and volume-capped. A fly central complex plus mushroom body needs about 250 × 250 × 250 µm³, beyond an 80 µm standard-resolution milling limit, so samples must be partitioned without losing traceable processes.
ocar.action: Xu, Pang, Hayworth, and Hess on bioRxiv (2019) describe enhanced FIB-SEM: expanding image volume more than four orders of magnitude from 10³ µm³ to 3 × 10⁷ µm³ at 8 × 8 × 8 nm³ voxels, optional 4 nm voxels, and years of continuous imaging. Hot-knife slabs (~20–25 µm) are imaged in parallel and stitched.
ocar.resolution: A male Drosophila VNC was cut into 25 slabs of 25 µm (220 × 200 × 600 µm³, ~2.6 × 10⁷ µm³) and imaged on six machines in about six months. A female hemi-brain of 250 × 250 × 250 µm³ (~1.6 × 10⁷ µm³) is described as containing ~25 × 10³ neurons and ~60 × 10⁶ synapses after segmentation. Estimated material loss between slabs is ~30 nm.
ocar.future_work: Maximum volume remains time-limited; hot-knife is described as incompatible with some heavy-metal stains and Durcupan, while PLT-LTS staining is noted to enable faster imaging. Mammalian volumes still exceed these fly examples.

summaries.beginner: A microscope that shaves tissue a few nanometers at a time makes beautiful 3D pictures but used to break down after days. This work keeps it running for months to years so much larger fly-brain pieces can be photographed at even detail in every direction.
summaries.intermediate: Xu et al. on bioRxiv (2019) enhance FIB-SEM for long, isotropic 8 nm (optionally 4 nm) imaging from 10³ to 3 × 10⁷ µm³. Hot-knife partitioning produced a Drosophila VNC (~2.6 × 10⁷ µm³, six machines, ~six months) and a hemi-brain (~1.6 × 10⁷ µm³). They argue high z-resolution aids automated tracing and cuts proofreading. Platforms are described as years-stable versus days for conventional FIB-SEM.
summaries.advanced: Neuron and synapse counts for the hemi-brain (~25,000 neurons, ~60 million synapses) refer to a segmented product, not proven in this methods preprint alone. Hot-knife adoption is limited by resin/stain compatibility as the authors state. 'Largest connectome in the world' is their 2019 framing. 4 nm mode trades speed for resolution.

plain_language_summary: A microscope that shaves tissue a few nanometers at a time makes beautiful 3D pictures but used to break down after days. This work keeps it running for months to years so much larger fly-brain pieces can be photographed at even detail in every direction.

ocar.opportunity: A complete synaptic inventory of one identified Drosophila antennal-lobe glomerulus, including local interneurons that had been hard to reconstruct, would be a template for the remaining glomeruli and for functional genetics of smell.
ocar.challenge: Local interneurons have dense multidirectional arbors that serial-section EM reconstructs poorly. Genetic screens of projection neurons may be unsaturated. Light-level candidate partners do not reliably equal synapses.
ocar.action: Horne, Langille, McLin, Wiederman, Lu, Xu, Plaza, Scheffer, Hess, and Meinertzhagen in eLife (2018) densely reconstruct all neurons in right-antennal-lobe glomerulus VA1v from FIB-SEM, including local interneurons, and publish a connectivity matrix.
ocar.resolution: They report more than 11,140 presynaptic sites and about 38,050 postsynaptic dendrites connecting 51 ipsilateral and 56 contralateral ORNs, 18 PNs, and 56 of more than 150 previously reported LNs. A matrix of 192 bodies with more than 50 connections accounts for 88% of the glomerulus's pre/postsynaptic sites. LNs are largely reciprocal and mixed pre/post except LN2V; PNs outnumber genetic-screen counts.
ocar.future_work: The resource is offered as proof of principle for the remaining ~50 glomeruli and as a heuristic for imaging, physiology, and computational models of insect olfaction.

summaries.beginner: One smell-processing bead in a fruit-fly antenna brain was mapped so every connection inside it is listed, including hard-to-trace local cells. The map is meant as a recipe for the rest of the smell center.
summaries.intermediate: Horne et al. in eLife (2018) report a FIB-SEM dense connectome of Drosophila glomerulus VA1v: >11,140 presynaptic sites, ~38,050 postsynaptic dendrites, 51+56 ORNs, 18 PNs, and 56 LNs. 192 bodies with >50 connections hold 88% of sites. ORNs are mostly presynaptic, PNs mostly postsynaptic; most LNs are reciprocal except LN2V. FIB-SEM z-resolution is credited for reconstructing LN arbors.
summaries.advanced: This is one glomerulus of the right antennal lobe, not the full lobe. 'Entire synaptic connectome' is within VA1v as reconstructed. PN counts exceeding genetic screens imply those screens were unsaturated, not that extra PNs were missed by EM. Reciprocity highlights in the matrix use a ≥3-synapse-each-way rule.

plain_language_summary: One smell-processing bead in a fruit-fly antenna brain was mapped so every connection inside it is listed, including hard-to-trace local cells. The map is meant as a recipe for the rest of the smell center.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation is the bottleneck for large connectomes, but challenge metrics (CREMI, SNEMI) on small ground-truth cubes often fail to predict whether a reconstruction preserves synapses and is usable at production scale.
ocar.challenge: Common scores ignore connectivity and can over-rate segmentations. Ground truth is scarce, so large-volume evaluation needs unsupervised clues. Edit-distance costs also depend on how proofreading is actually done.
ocar.action: Plaza and Funke in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018) introduce connectivity-aware metrics (synapse connectivity and completeness), unsupervised cues (orphan-fragment percentage, self-loop concentrations from failures), and a scalable DVID/Spark software-and-visualization stack. They evaluate on two relatively large public ground-truth datasets.
ocar.resolution: Connectivity-based metrics indicate that fully automatic reconstructions still need substantial improvement, matching practical experience. They find data can be downsampled without large effects on important metrics, and that two segmentations can be compared without ground truth by inspecting the largest metric-driven differences.
ocar.future_work: They advocate more failure-mode metrics rather than a single champion score; choice of metric should follow the application (edit distance for proofreading cost, fragmentation for over-segmentation).

summaries.beginner: Scoreboards that grade computer tracings of brain pictures often ignore whether the wiring list is still right. This paper adds tests that ask whether connections survive, and software to run those tests on bigger volumes.
summaries.intermediate: Plaza and Funke in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018) argue CREMI/SNEMI-style metrics miss downstream connectivity. They add synapse connectivity/completeness scores, orphan and self-loop measures usable without ground truth, and a scalable evaluation/visualization framework tested on two large public ground-truth sets. They conclude automatic segmentation is not yet sufficient for fully automatic reconstructions.
summaries.advanced: The paper is agnostic about a single best metric. Unsupervised orphan/self-loop measures can flag problems but are not a substitute for synapse-level truth. 'Two relatively large' ground-truth sets are not named in the selected extract. Downsampling invariance is stated qualitatively.

plain_language_summary: Scoreboards that grade computer tracings of brain pictures often ignore whether the wiring list is still right. This paper adds tests that ask whether connections survive, and software to run those tests on bigger volumes.

ocar.opportunity: Food intake and metabolic homeostasis depend on how many sensory paths are funneled onto shared motor, modulatory, and neuroendocrine outputs. A synaptic map of those paths in a whole larval CNS would show whether reflexes are simple one-hop circuits or stacked on longer routes.
ocar.challenge: How one path is selected among many possible outputs remains open. Nervous-system complexity usually forces partial maps. Feeding mixes enteric, pharyngeal, and external senses with motor, serotonergic, and endocrine effectors, plus a separate memory circuit.
ocar.action: Miroschnikow, Schlegel, Schoofs, Hueckesfeld, Li, Schneider-Mizell, Fetter, Truman, Cardona, and Pankratz in eLife (2018) reconstruct from a whole-CNS EM volume the synaptic map of Drosophila larval feeding-related input and output neurons.
ocar.resolution: Inputs converge on seven sensory synaptic compartments in the CNS (SEZ). Monosynaptic connections from a subset of compartments cover motor, modulatory, and neuroendocrine targets in overlapping domains (ACa, AVa, AVp). Polysynaptic routes overlay those reflexes; a different sensory set reaches mushroom-body calyx, with MB output neurons targeting interneurons that contact feeding outputs.
ocar.future_work: They interpret the architecture as an elemental feeding reflex plus superimposed control paths, a template for other instinctive behaviors.

summaries.beginner: A young fruit fly must eat using sensors in the gut, mouth, and skin that all talk to pumping muscles and hormone cells. This map shows some sensors plug straight into those outputs while other routes wander through extra cells, including a learning center.
summaries.intermediate: Miroschnikow et al. in eLife (2018) reconstruct a Drosophila larval feeding connectome from a whole-CNS EM volume. Seven SEZ sensory compartments receive enteric, pharyngeal, and external inputs. Overlapping monosynaptic domains target pharyngeal motor, serotonergic, and neuroendocrine neurons; polysynaptic paths and a distinct MB-calyx sensory set are superimposed. Most elemental-circuit sensors are enteric.
summaries.advanced: This is the feeding-related sensory–output map, not the entire larval connectome. 'Elemental circuit' is an interpretive label for irreducibly short connections. Small somatosensory monosynaptic paths to mouth-hook/head-tilt motor neurons mix feeding and locomotion. Functional path selection is inferred from anatomy.

plain_language_summary: A young fruit fly must eat using sensors in the gut, mouth, and skin that all talk to pumping muscles and hormone cells. This map shows some sensors plug straight into those outputs while other routes wander through extra cells, including a learning center.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics is treated as a cluster-scale machine-learning problem, yet data already arrive at terabytes per hour. If algorithms and multicore engineering can match microscope pace on one lab server, labs would not have to ship data to the cloud.
ocar.challenge: It has been assumed that extracting graphs from EM will need mass storage, CPU/GPU farms, and months to years. Popular packages show 50- to 100-fold GPU-over-CPU speedups, encouraging cluster thinking. Trivial MapReduce splits fail when stages must communicate.
ocar.action: Matveev, Meirovitch, Saribekyan, Jakubiuk, Kaler, Ódor, Budden, Zlateski, and Shavit at PPoPP (2017) present a high-throughput connectomics-on-demand system on a commodity multicore machine with fewer than 100 cores, including a carefully engineered CNN (XNN), demonstrated on Kasthuri data.
ocar.resolution: They report connectome extraction at the terabyte-per-hour pace of modern EM. On an 18-core 2.4 GHz Haswell chip, XNN is only 2–3× slower than gpuZNN or Neon on a Titan X; a 4-core Skylake is 4–6× slower than that GPU. They argue a single multicore can outperform existing CPU- and GPU-based clusters on this pipeline.
ocar.future_work: The case study is meant to remind the community that multicore performance engineering can beat default cluster scaling for tightly coupled image pipelines; it is not a claim that all big-data problems belong on one box.

summaries.beginner: Many people assume mapping a brain from electron-microscope movies needs a warehouse of computers. These authors show that careful programming on one ordinary many-core machine can keep up with the microscope's flood of pictures.
summaries.intermediate: Matveev et al. at PPoPP (2017) engineer a multicore (<100 cores) streaming connectomics pipeline claimed to run at terabyte-per-hour EM rates. On Kasthuri data they contrast this with cluster assumptions. After optimization, their CPU CNN is only a few-fold slower than a high-end GPU, inverting naive 50–100× GPU/CPU package ratios.
summaries.advanced: Throughput is for their pipeline on Kasthuri-scale data, not a proofread whole-brain connectome. GPU comparisons use specific libraries and chips (Haswell, Skylake, Titan X, Neon, gpuZNN). 'Outperform clusters' is their case-study claim. Proofreading is outside this systems paper.

plain_language_summary: Many people assume mapping a brain from electron-microscope movies needs a warehouse of computers. These authors show that careful programming on one ordinary many-core machine can keep up with the microscope's flood of pictures.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM cell segmentation always leaves merge and split errors. If software can point people at likely mistakes, proofreading could become a series of yes/no decisions instead of a visual search through volumes.
ocar.challenge: Prior work identified visual search for errors as the interactive bottleneck. Merge errors are especially hard for both novices and experts. Fully automatic correction must not add more damage than it removes.
ocar.action: Haehn, Kaynig, Tompkin, Lichtman, and Pfister at CVPR (2018) train two CNNs on automatic-segmentation errors versus expert ground truth to recommend candidate merges and splits from large context around boundaries. Users accept or reject; a fully automatic mode uses a probability threshold. They compare novices, experts, and prior tools on multiple datasets.
ocar.resolution: Yes/no corrections reduce variation of information 7.5× faster than previous proofreading methods. An oracle reaches median VI 0.342 (SD 0.03) after 800 corrections, near the best-possible 0.334. Automatic merge selection at pt = 0.95 on 50 L. Cylinder sections yielded precision/recall 0.82/0.73 (F1 0.77) with negligible net VI effect because true and false corrections mixed.
ocar.future_work: They conclude automatic proofreading can further cut human labor and release the framework at rhoana.org/guidedproofreading/.

summaries.beginner: People who fix computer tracings of brain cells spend most of their time just finding the mistakes. This method has a network suggest likely cuts and joins so a person mostly answers yes or no.
summaries.intermediate: Haehn et al. at CVPR (2018) present guided proofreading: CNNs propose merge and split candidates from boundary context. Interactive yes/no decisions are reported to reduce VI 7.5× faster than prior methods. Automatic mode and novice/expert studies are included; merge errors remain hard (novices marked 1.9 true merges in one study). Open tools are at rhoana.org/guidedproofreading/.
summaries.advanced: The 7.5× figure is a VI-reduction-rate comparison, not wall-clock on production teravoxel volumes. Automatic merge correction at pt = 0.95 had mixed true/false edits and negligible VI change. Best-possible VI 0.334 is overlap-with-ground-truth, not biological truth. Datasets include L. Cylinder among others named in experiments.

plain_language_summary: People who fix computer tracings of brain cells spend most of their time just finding the mistakes. This method has a network suggest likely cuts and joins so a person mostly answers yes or no.

ocar.opportunity: Defining how neuronal networks are organized at the cellular scale—micro-connectomics—is a central challenge. Graph-theoretical descriptions, especially those inspired by Cajal's conservation ideas, offer a common language for small intact nervous systems and samples from larger brains.
ocar.challenge: It remains unclear which topological features of micro-connectomes reflect an economical trade-off between biological cost and functional value, versus historical or technical accident.
ocar.action: Schröter, Paulsen, and Bullmore review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2017) graph-theoretical parameters of micro-connectome topology. They summarize results from intact small organisms and from samples of larger nervous systems, then evaluate evidence for cost–value trade-offs.
ocar.resolution: They conclude that various results suggest many aspects of neuronal network organization are the outcome of competition between biological cost and functional value.
ocar.future_work: The review frames further micro-connectomic mapping as a way to test how general that economical trade-off is across species and scales.

summaries.beginner: Scientists can now list which tiny brain cells connect in small animals and in bits of larger brains. This review asks whether those wiring patterns look like a compromise between saving biological resources and doing useful computations.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2017), Schröter, Paulsen, and Bullmore survey micro-connectomics through graph theory, linking the program to Ramón y Cajal's conservation laws. They cover intact small organisms and samples from larger nervous systems and argue for an economical trade-off between biological cost and functional value in network organization.
summaries.advanced: Selected PDF text does not match this catalog paper (extract is Jin, Li, and Wang 2025, Network Neuroscience, on morphological similarity networks). Summaries follow the catalog abstract only. This is a review; 'various results suggest' is qualitative. No new connectome is presented.

plain_language_summary: Scientists can now list which tiny brain cells connect in small animals and in bits of larger brains. This review asks whether those wiring patterns look like a compromise between saving biological resources and doing useful computations.

ocar.opportunity: Nanometer EM produces petabytes that must be aligned, labeled, proofread, and turned into graphs, and every step needs interactive visualization. Middleware that hides data wrangling would let labs ship new viewers instead of new storage stacks.
ocar.challenge: Connectomics sits at both nano and peta scales. Each pipeline stage has distinct visualization needs (2D/3D, editing, graphs). Low-level I/O otherwise dominates development time.
ocar.action: Haehn, Hoffer, Matejek, Suissa-Peleg, Al-Awami, Kamentsky, Gonda, Meng, Zhang, Schalek, Wilson, Parag, Beyer, Kaynig, Jones, Tompkin, Hadwiger, Lichtman, and Pfister in Informatics (2017) present BUTTERFLY middleware plus open-source web apps spanning data management, queries, 2D/3D views, Dojo editing, and graph analysis, with measured rendering throughput.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate scalability and extendability across the typical workflow and release the stack as open source. Butterfly is described as abstracting massive-data problems so scientists can focus on connectomics rather than I/O.
ocar.future_work: They expect more sophisticated visualizations as the field matures and hope Butterfly remains a common substrate.

summaries.beginner: Petabyte electron-microscope stacks are hard even to open, let alone to edit and graph. This paper describes shared plumbing and web tools so people can browse, fix, and analyze those stacks without rewriting the storage layer each time.
summaries.intermediate: Haehn et al. in Informatics (2017) introduce Butterfly middleware for interactive connectomics visualization, with applications for storage, queries, 2D/3D viewing, proofreading (Dojo), and graphs. They report design choices, combined-use scenarios, and rendering-throughput measurements, and release the software open source.
summaries.advanced: Throughput numbers are not in the selected extract. Butterfly is middleware plus example apps, not a segmentation algorithm. Dojo split/merge examples illustrate editing, not a completed connectome. NSF/IARPA/KAUST funding is acknowledged; organism/dataset are unspecified here.

plain_language_summary: Petabyte electron-microscope stacks are hard even to open, let alone to edit and graph. This paper describes shared plumbing and web tools so people can browse, fix, and analyze those stacks without rewriting the storage layer each time.

ocar.opportunity: Neurosecretory centers influence physiology through peptides as well as synapses. Mapping cell types, synapses, and peptide–receptor pairs in one center would show how chemical and synaptic brains overlay.
ocar.challenge: EM connectomics misses volume transmission. Overlaying peptides and receptors on synapses has been done only for relatively simple circuits. Single-cell RNA-seq scores transcripts, not peptide release or neuronal activation, and a small head dataset cannot capture long-range neuroendocrine signaling.
ocar.action: Williams, Verasztó, Jasek, Conzelmann, Shahidi, Bauknecht, Mirabeau, and Jékely in eLife (2017) reconstruct 78 neurosecretory neurons and their synapses in the larval Platynereis dumerilii brain and combine that map with spatially registered single-cell transcriptomes of peptide–receptor pairs, plus an experimental test of one pair (achatin).
ocar.resolution: The anterior neurosecretory center (ANS) expresses many neuropeptides, including hypothalamic orthologs and receptors, with sparsely connected peptide networks linking specific subsets. Synaptic connectivity in the ANS is low; most peptidergic signaling appears internal, including autocrine peptide–receptor co-expression (allatotropin/orexin, NPY4, achatin, and others). Achatin is shown to couple neurosecretory and synaptic signaling.
ocar.future_work: Larger single-cell datasets and other species could extend long-range endocrine maps; the authors treat peptide–receptor matching as a way to wire complex chemical networks even with few synapses.

summaries.beginner: Some brain centers talk more with secreted chemical messages than with classic synapses. In a marine worm larva, researchers listed those cells, their few synapses, and which peptide signals they could send and receive.
summaries.intermediate: Williams et al. in eLife (2017) map 78 neurosecretory neurons in larval Platynereis by TEM and overlay peptide–receptor expression from spatially mapped scRNA-seq. Peptide networks are sparse and specific; the ANS is weakly synaptic and peptide-rich, with several autocrine pairs. Experimental analysis of achatin shows a peptide can couple neurosecretory and synaptic signaling.
summaries.advanced: Peptidergic links are inferred from mRNA, not measured release. The scRNA-seq set is a relatively small head sample. 'Entire neurosecretory center' is the reconstructed ANS of this larva. Catalog organism 'other' / DS22 Platynereis matches. Achatin is one tested pair among many inferred channels.

plain_language_summary: Some brain centers talk more with secreted chemical messages than with classic synapses. In a marine worm larva, researchers listed those cells, their few synapses, and which peptide signals they could send and receive.

ocar.opportunity: Direction-selective T4 cells are the ON motion detectors of Drosophila, but models (Hassenstein–Reichardt versus Barlow–Levick) outrun known anatomy. A comprehensive EM input map would show which circuits could implement preferred-direction enhancement, null-direction suppression, or both.
ocar.challenge: Exact neuronal implementation of elementary motion detection remains imperfectly known. A prior report of spatial offset between Mi1 and Tm3 inputs needed checking. Dense reconstruction of seven medulla columns is labor-intensive.
ocar.action: Takemura, Nern, Chklovskii, Scheffer, Rubin, and Meinertzhagen in eLife (2017) reconstruct T4 circuits with FIB-SEM (10 nm isotropic voxels from 2.5 nm milling, 32,000 images; seven medulla columns in ~30,000 µm³) using automated segmentation plus ~6,000 person-hours of Raveler proofreading of synapses.
ocar.resolution: They report the complete set of T4 input types: putative excitatory inputs cluster on dendrite shafts and inhibitory inputs at bases. Mi1 and Tm3 still provide most contacts, but the previously reported spatial offset between them is not reproduced. Anatomy is compatible with both HR-type enhancement and BL-type suppression, matching contemporaneous imaging in T4 and T5.
ocar.future_work: They note inhibition could serve gain control (for example CT1) rather than direction selectivity alone; EM findings are to be combined with specific functional tests.

summaries.beginner: How a fly's eye tells which way something moves has been modeled for decades without a full parts list. This paper traces every input onto the key motion-sensing cells and finds wiring that could support more than one classic model.
summaries.intermediate: Takemura et al. in eLife (2017) reconstruct ON-motion T4 inputs in Drosophila medulla with isotropic 10 nm FIB-SEM across seven columns. Excitatory-type inputs cluster on shafts, inhibitory-type at dendritic bases. Mi1 and Tm3 dominate synapses but without the earlier spatial offset. The connectome offers candidate substrates for both Hassenstein–Reichardt and Barlow–Levick detectors.
summaries.advanced: FIB-SEM voxels are 10 nm after summing four 2.5 nm slices, not the 8 nm of some later fly volumes. Failure to reproduce Mi1–Tm3 offset is a direct conflict with a previous study by overlapping authors and should be cited as such. 'Comprehensive' is for T4 inputs in seven columns, not the whole optic lobe. Direction selectivity still requires physiology; anatomy is 'qualified to implement' both models.

plain_language_summary: How a fly's eye tells which way something moves has been modeled for decades without a full parts list. This paper traces every input onto the key motion-sensing cells and finds wiring that could support more than one classic model.

ocar.opportunity: Membrane segmentation can individuate neurons, but connectivity graphs also need synapses. A fast, accurate synapse detector that keeps up with multi-beam EM would close the streaming-connectomics loop on lab CPUs.
ocar.challenge: Synapses are compositional (cleft plus asymmetric vesicles) yet deep nets are usually asked to learn the full combination. Prior ConvNet synapse detectors were too slow (Vesicle-CNN would take many years on 245 GB S1; Vesicle-RF more than a week).
ocar.action: Santurkar, Budden, Matveev, Berlin, Saribekyan, Meirovitch, and Shavit on arXiv (2017) train light ConvNets on membranes, clefts, and vesicles from 100 EM samples and compose them with biology-derived heuristics, optimized for shared-memory multicore CPUs.
ocar.resolution: They report 7% higher recall and 5% higher F1 than previous state of the art, a 20-fold speedup versus the previous fastest implementations (and 11,000-fold versus Vesicle-CNN). They reconstruct a directed connectome from a 245 GB anisotropic mouse somatosensory-cortex (S1) volume in 9.7 hours on one CPU system.
ocar.future_work: They present this as closing the gap toward microscope-pace synapse detection by about two orders of magnitude and suggest compositional ConvNets for other segmentation tasks.

summaries.beginner: Finding the contact points between brain cells is slower than tracing the cells themselves. This method teaches small networks to see membranes, gaps, and little packets separately, then combines those clues with simple biological rules so a regular computer can finish a large mouse-cortex volume in hours.
summaries.intermediate: Santurkar et al. (arXiv 2017) detect synapses compositionally: light CNNs for membranes, clefts, and vesicles trained on 100 EM samples, plus heuristics. They claim +7% recall and +5% F1 versus prior SOTA, 20× versus the previous fastest method, and a directed graph from 245 GB mouse S1 in 9.7 hours on one multicore CPU.
summaries.advanced: 'First complete, directed connectome' refers to this 245 GB anisotropic S1 stack, not a whole brain. Speedups are versus Vesicle-RF/Vesicle-CNN as named. Training on 100 samples is small; generalization beyond S1 is untested here. Directed edges inherit whatever polarity the vesicle/cleft heuristic assigns.

plain_language_summary: Finding the contact points between brain cells is slower than tracing the cells themselves. This method teaches small networks to see membranes, gaps, and little packets separately, then combines those clues with simple biological rules so a regular computer can finish a large mouse-cortex volume in hours.

ocar.opportunity: Petabyte streaming EM needs pixel-level segmentation at near terabyte-per-hour microscope pace. A two-pass pipeline that is first fast then carefully corrective could turn cubic-millimeter acquisition from a years-long compute problem into hours on one multicore machine.
ocar.challenge: Existing algorithms can be relatively accurate but unacceptably slow—years for a cubic millimeter. Fast-pass methods raise new issues: shallow nets, parallel watershed, and object merging, plus how to find morphological errors without a full slow pass.
ocar.action: Meirovitch, Matveev, Saribekyan, Budden, Rolnick, Ódor, Knowles-Barley, Jones, Pfister, Lichtman, and Shavit on arXiv (2016) describe a multi-pass shared-memory pipeline: a fast pass then an iterative slow pass to correct errors, including a sparse slow-pass reconstruction algorithm.
ocar.resolution: They reconstruct the full Kasthuri et al. dataset (463 GB; 120,000 cubic microns) from images to skeletons in hours on one multicore machine, versus weeks previously on larger distributed systems, at near multi-beam terabyte-per-hour pace.
ocar.future_work: They suggest new morphological-error detectors and further slow-pass refinement as the path to higher accuracy without giving up streaming throughput.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can now photograph brain tissue faster than ordinary analysis software can keep up. This preprint describes a two-speed computer pipeline: a quick first look, then a slower cleanup, so a single lab machine can finish a large published volume in hours.
summaries.intermediate: Meirovitch et al. (arXiv 2016) present a multi-pass connectomics pipeline for shared-memory multicores. A fast pass is followed by a slower error-correcting pass. They report reconstructing Kasthuri et al. (463 GB, 120,000 µm³) to skeletons in hours on one machine rather than weeks on larger clusters, aiming at terabyte-per-hour EM rates.
summaries.advanced: Selected PDF text does not match this catalog paper (extract is Wen et al. on bit fully convolutional networks for VOC/Cityscapes). Summaries follow the catalog abstract only. 'Hours' versus 'weeks' is not broken into hardware specs here. Output is skeletons, not a fully proofread synapse graph. Catalog dataset tags include Kasthuri and MICrONS; the reported reconstruction is Kasthuri.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can now photograph brain tissue faster than ordinary analysis software can keep up. This preprint describes a two-speed computer pipeline: a quick first look, then a slower cleanup, so a single lab machine can finish a large published volume in hours.

ocar.opportunity: Behavior comes from a synaptic network, so a Drosophila central-nervous-system connectome is a major objective. Light-microscopic cell-type maps already show which neurons come close; EM can turn proximity into synapses and predict unexpected pathways.
ocar.challenge: Proximity is not partnership: anatomical synapses often reveal pathways that candidate pairs miss. Degeneracy can foil cell-by-cell behavioral knockout tests. Work is furthest along in optic neuropils, not the whole CNS.
ocar.action: Meinertzhagen in Journal of Neurogenetics (2016) offers a short perspective on Drosophila connectomics, especially Janelia efforts, contrasting EM (notably FIB-SEM) with genetic light-level reconstructions, and placing fly work beside the inner plexiform layer of vertebrate retina and the 30-year-old C. elegans connectome.
ocar.resolution: He argues that ultrastructural partnerships are a heuristic for function and a way to predict interactions not obvious from experiments, and that circuit motifs and higher-order network properties are additional uses beyond single-cell interruption.
ocar.future_work: The piece anticipates parallel dense reconstructions in other systems and completion of fly CNS maps beyond the optic lobes.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly brains are small enough that a full wiring list is becoming thinkable. This short essay explains why electron-microscope synapses, not just which cells sit near each other, are what you need to guess how the fly computes.
summaries.intermediate: Meinertzhagen in Journal of Neurogenetics (2016) perspectives Drosophila connectomics, emphasizing optic neuropils and FIB-SEM versus light-microscopic candidate partners. He stresses that synapses often reveal unexpected pathways, that degeneracy can hide single-cell causal tests, and that fly EM work parallels vertebrate retinal inner plexiform studies and extends the long-available C. elegans connectome.
summaries.advanced: Selected PDF text does not match this catalog paper (extract is Tanaka and Clark 2022 eNeuro on lobula visual projection neurons). Summaries follow the catalog abstract only. This is perspective, not a new volume. Catalog organism/dataset tags include C. elegans and mouse retina as comparison systems named in the abstract, not as the paper's primary reconstructions.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly brains are small enough that a full wiring list is becoming thinkable. This short essay explains why electron-microscope synapses, not just which cells sit near each other, are what you need to guess how the fly computes.

ocar.opportunity: Standard EM neuron segmentation splits boundary detection from watershed-style grouping, so the learned step never directly optimizes object identity. An end-to-end recurrent net that grows one segment at a time could replace that pipeline.
ocar.challenge: Object number and size vary wildly in neuropil. Inference cost scales with volume and with how many objects sit in the field of view, and overlapping fields of view reprocess voxels. Movement of the field of view during training and inference is still heuristic.
ocar.action: Januszewski, Maitin-Shepard, Li, Kornfeld, Denk, and Jain introduce flood-filling networks on arXiv (2016): a recurrent 3D convolutional net that iteratively fills individual segments from raw EM, demonstrated on connectomic volume EM.
ocar.resolution: They report substantial accuracy gains over other contemporary methods on a challenging 3D EM reconstruction task and argue FFNs can replace multi-step pipelines with one end-to-end network. On a densely skeletonized subvolume, FFN inference cost is 4.6 PFLOP versus about 0.14 PFLOP for a 3D affinity-graph CNN; typically 2–3 objects occupy the field of view, and voxels are processed multiple times (42–75% FoV overlap).
ocar.future_work: They outline cheaper architectures (U-Net-like bottlenecks, strided convs, larger steps, split mask/image branches), ultrastructure-aware training, better handling of extremely thin processes, and a learned FoV-movement policy.

summaries.beginner: Usual computer programs first find cell edges and then flood-fill the insides as a separate step. This network grows each cell from the raw 3D picture in one learned loop, aiming to trace tangled brain wires more accurately.
summaries.intermediate: Januszewski et al. (arXiv 2016) present flood-filling networks: a recurrent 3D CNN that emits one object at a time from raw EM. They report large accuracy gains versus then-standard boundary-plus-watershed pipelines on connectomic data. Compute is higher (4.6 vs 0.14 PFLOP on one subvolume) because multiple overlapping passes visit each object.
summaries.advanced: This preprint predates the 2018 Nature Methods FFN paper; headline path-length numbers from that later paper are not in this extract and are not used. 'Substantially improve accuracy' is not given as a named metric here. Cost figures are for one densely skeletonized subvolume. FoV movement remains heuristic in this version.

plain_language_summary: Usual computer programs first find cell edges and then flood-fill the insides as a separate step. This network grows each cell from the raw 3D picture in one learned loop, aiming to trace tangled brain wires more accurately.

ocar.opportunity: A structure–function model of the nervous system would mechanistically link mind, brain, and behavior. A necessary foundation is a connectome: a complete matrix of structural connections among defined nodes, described at nested spatial grains.
ocar.challenge: Connections can be stated as macroconnections between regions, mesoconnections between neuron types, microconnections between individual neurons, and nanoconnections at synapses. The hardest present problem is extracting knowledge from vast data, not only collecting more.
ocar.action: Swanson and Lichtman in Annual Review of Neuroscience (2016) survey this nested program from fifth-century macro-anatomy through Cajal's meso/micro revolution to mid-twentieth-century electron microscopy at the nanolevel.
ocar.resolution: They organize the historical arc as successive resolution of the same connectivity question and identify extracting understanding from large datasets as today's central challenge.
ocar.future_work: The review treats a connectome as necessary but not sufficient for a structure–function model; function still has to be linked at each nested level.

summaries.beginner: A wiring list of the brain can mean very different things: regions, cell types, single cells, or actual synapses. This review walks through that ladder of detail from classical anatomy to electron microscopy and asks how to turn the flood of maps into understanding.
summaries.intermediate: Swanson and Lichtman in Annual Review of Neuroscience (2016) define connectomes at four nested grains (macro, meso, micro, nano) and trace the program from ancient regional maps through Cajal to EM synapses. They argue a complete connection matrix is necessary but not sufficient for linking mind, brain, and behavior, and that knowledge extraction is now the bottleneck.
summaries.advanced: Selected PDF text does not match this catalog paper (extract is Meirovitch et al. 2026 Nature Methods SmartEM). Summaries follow the catalog abstract only. This is a historical/conceptual review, not a methods benchmark. 'Complete matrix' is an aspirational definition at each level.

plain_language_summary: A wiring list of the brain can mean very different things: regions, cell types, single cells, or actual synapses. This review walks through that ladder of detail from classical anatomy to electron microscopy and asks how to turn the flood of maps into understanding.

ocar.opportunity: Cellular-resolution connectomics needs scalable image analysis with little user intervention. Deep residual architectures that improve membrane (and other) segmentation would reduce that bottleneck.
ocar.challenge: High-throughput nanoscale EM produces more imagery than manual annotation can match. Segmentation accuracy still limits fully automatic reconstructions.
ocar.action: Quan, Hildebrand, and Jeong introduce FusionNet (catalog year 2016; Frontiers in Computer Science DOI): a deep fully residual convolutional network that combines semantic-segmentation and residual-network ideas with summation-based skip connections, trained for EM neuronal structures.
ocar.resolution: They report improved segmentation accuracy relative to several popular EM methods and show flexibility on two tasks: cell-membrane segmentation and cell-nucleus segmentation. Summation skip connections are credited for enabling a deeper architecture.
ocar.future_work: The architecture is offered as a general segmentation tool for connectomic EM; broader adoption would still require integration into full agglomeration and proofreading pipelines.

summaries.beginner: Computers must outline every cell in electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue. This network uses extra residual shortcuts so a very deep model can still learn, and the authors test it on drawing cell membranes and nuclei.
summaries.intermediate: Quan, Hildebrand, and Jeong (2016; Frontiers of Computer Science DOI in this catalog) present FusionNet, a residual semantic-segmentation CNN with summation skip connections for connectomics EM. They compare it with several popular EM segmentation methods and demonstrate both membrane and nucleus segmentation.
summaries.advanced: Selected PDF text does not match this catalog paper (extract is Konstein and Tyutin on symplectic reflection algebras). Summaries follow the catalog abstract only. No numeric scores appear in the abstract. Catalog year 2016 versus 2021 Frontiers DOI likely reflects preprint versus journal version. Organism/dataset are unspecified.

plain_language_summary: Computers must outline every cell in electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue. This network uses extra residual shortcuts so a very deep model can still learn, and the authors test it on drawing cell membranes and nuclei.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput serial-section EM now captures complete specimens up to cubic-millimeter, multi-terabyte scale. Precise registration of thousands of sections is required before circuits can be traced.
ocar.challenge: Biological content changes rapidly between sections and distortion is unavoidable, so phase-only or Pearson correlation often fail. Adjacent-pair matching can drift. Anatomically true shape (for example a bent zebrafish) is not the same as the lowest-energy image match.
ocar.action: Wetzel, Bakal, Dittrich, Hildebrand, Morgan, and Lichtman at AIPR (2016) introduce SWiFT-IR: FFT registration that whitening-adjusts spatial frequency response to maximize a signal-to-noise alignment score, then iterates projections through multiple sections in a multi-resolution pyramid, using anatomical constraints. They apply it to mouse and zebrafish wafer-mapper ssEM from Harvard.
ocar.resolution: They argue the SNR-based match is more robust than phase-only or Pearson correlation, enabling multi-section projection alignment that stays smooth across widely varying content, including full-cross-section zebrafish. An example mouse visual-thalamus set is 10,000 sections, ~100 Tvoxels, 4 nm/pixel, ~400 µm square sections stitched from 16 tiles.
ocar.future_work: They stress that external shape priors (block shape, optical images, micro-CT) are needed when the scientific goal is true distances or phenotype, not merely pairwise image agreement.

summaries.beginner: Thousands of ultra-thin electron-microscope slices must be stacked so the same wires line up. This method tunes the matching process to be less fooled by changing tissue patterns, then looks through several slices at once so the stack stays smooth.
summaries.intermediate: Wetzel et al. at AIPR (2016) present SWiFT-IR for ssEM registration using FFT signal whitening and a signal-to-noise match score, with multi-section projection and pyramid iteration. They register mouse and zebrafish wafer-mapper volumes. A mouse visual-thalamus example comprises 10,000 sections at 4 nm/pixel (~100 Tvoxels). Alignment is treated as mandatory before tracing.
summaries.advanced: Robustness versus Pearson/POC is argued from matched-filter theory and case studies, not a single leaderboard number in the selected text. Multi-terabyte cubic-millimeter capture is the motivating regime. External anatomical constraints are required for metric fidelity. Catalog datasets include MICrONS and zebrafish; the named example is mouse visual thalamus plus zebrafish cross-section.

plain_language_summary: Thousands of ultra-thin electron-microscope slices must be stacked so the same wires line up. This method tunes the matching process to be less fooled by changing tissue patterns, then looks through several slices at once so the stack stays smooth.

ocar.opportunity: A cubic millimeter of EM is about 1 PB and cannot be annotated by hand. Updating a dense automatic segmentation pipeline with modern membrane CNNs and agglomeration would cut proofreading on existing mouse volumes and provide public benchmarks.
ocar.challenge: Earlier Rhoana stages needed higher-quality membrane maps and 3D agglomeration. One cortex set had conflicting annotators and a crop smaller than the default U-Net field of view. LGN contrast is lower and artifactual.
ocar.action: Knowles-Barley, Kaynig, Jones, Wilson, Morgan, Lee, Berger, Kasthuri, Lichtman, and Pfister on arXiv (2016) update Rhoana to RhoanaNet: U-Net membrane probabilities plus Gala agglomeration of 2D segments into 3D objects, run on four densely annotated mouse datasets (two cortex, cerebellum, LGN), with all data public at rhoana.org.
ocar.resolution: Best information-theoretic VF-scores are 0.9054 and 0.9182 on the cortex sets, 0.9438 on LGN, and 0.9150 on cerebellum (Table 1 also reports Rand scores). They describe qualitative 3D improvement and automatic processing of very large volumes.
ocar.future_work: Further quality and throughput gains plus informed proofreading strategies are stated as still necessary; the open benchmarks are for others to beat.

summaries.beginner: Tracing every wire in a cubic millimeter of mouse brain by hand would be impractical. This updated software pipeline paints membranes with a modern network, glues slices into 3D cells, and publishes the test pictures so other labs can compare.
summaries.intermediate: Knowles-Barley et al. (arXiv 2016) present RhoanaNet: U-Net boundaries and Gala agglomeration, succeeding Kaynig et al. 2015. On four dense mouse EM sets they report VI F-scores of 0.9054 and 0.9182 (cortex), 0.9438 (LGN), and 0.9150 (cerebellum). Code and annotations are at rhoana.org. A cubic millimeter is cited as ~1 PB.
summaries.advanced: Abstract typo '09182' is 0.9182 in the table. Rand and VI metrics disagree in ranking (LGN Rand VF-score 0.7744 vs VI 0.9438); do not cite one as 'the' score. ECS cortex used a reduced 540×540 U-Net input. Results are on four benchmark cubes, not a cubic millimeter production run.

plain_language_summary: Tracing every wire in a cubic millimeter of mouse brain by hand would be impractical. This updated software pipeline paints membranes with a modern network, glues slices into 3D cells, and publishes the test pictures so other labs can compare.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic wiring is only one layer of C. elegans communication. Mapping monoamine and neuropeptide extrasynaptic links onto the known 302-neuron synaptic and gap-junction connectome would show how neuromodulation sits on the wired circuit.
ocar.challenge: Volume transmission occurs mostly off the synaptic graph and is invisible to high-throughput EM. Overlap between wireless and wired links is low, so integration sites must be found as multilayer motifs rather than shared edges. Peptide coverage here is only a subset; valence and strength of inferred links are largely unknown.
ocar.action: Bentley, Branicky, Barnes, Chew, Yemini, Bullmore, Vértes, and Schafer in PLoS Computational Biology (2016) compile putative monoamine connections and a partial neuropeptide connectome from new and published gene-expression data, then analyze each layer's topology and multilink motifs with the White-style synaptic/gap-junction network.
ocar.resolution: The monoamine network is highly disassortative and star-like with a rich club of broadcasting hubs suited to global state; the neuropeptide network is more recurrent and clustered. Despite low overlap with wired connections, significant multilink motifs mark where amines and peptides likely modulate synapses (including multilayer hubs such as RIM and DVA).
ocar.future_work: They offer the multiplex map as a prototype for extrasynaptic layers in larger brains, while noting that more complete peptide–receptor coverage and functional signs are still needed.

summaries.beginner: The worm's famous wiring diagram lists synapses, but cells also broadcast chemical messages that never use those contacts. This paper sketches those wireless monoamine and peptide networks and where they plug into the wired circuit.
summaries.intermediate: Bentley et al. in PLoS Computational Biology (2016) add monoamine and partial neuropeptide layers to the C. elegans connectome using expression of biosynthetic genes and receptors. Monoamine topology is star-like with a broadcasting rich club; neuropeptides are clustered and reciprocal. Multilink motifs and hubs (RIM, DVA) indicate integration with synaptic and gap-junction layers despite little edge overlap.
summaries.advanced: Extrasynaptic edges are putative from expression, not EM. Neuropeptide mapping is explicitly partial. 'Highly significant' motifs are statistical overrepresentation, not measured physiology. The 302-neuron hermaphrodite synaptic connectome is the wired substrate. Catalog DS01 matches.

plain_language_summary: The worm's famous wiring diagram lists synapses, but cells also broadcast chemical messages that never use those contacts. This paper sketches those wireless monoamine and peptide networks and where they plug into the wired circuit.

ocar.opportunity: Anatomical connectomes still lack a system-wide chemical map of which transmitters each neuron uses. Charting every cholinergic neuron in both C. elegans sexes would show how acetylcholine is deployed across the White/Jarrell wiring diagrams and how that identity is transcriptionally built.
ocar.challenge: Even in C. elegans, neurotransmitter identities had not been fully mapped at single-neuron resolution in both sexes. Acetylcholine can be excitatory or, via ACh-gated anion channels, inhibitory—so presence of ACh is not a simple excitatory tag.
ocar.action: Pereira, Kratsios, Serrano-Saiz, Sheftel, Mayo, Hall, White, LeBoeuf, Garcia, Alon, and Hobert in eLife (2015) systematically map all cholinergic neuron types in male and hermaphrodite C. elegans, place ACh in connectome motifs, score ACh-gated anion-channel expression, and identify transcriptional regulators of cholinergic identity and circuit assembly.
ocar.resolution: Acetylcholine is the most broadly used transmitter in the nematode (unlike glutamate's dominance in vertebrate CNS). They describe a sexually dimorphic glutamatergic-to-cholinergic switch in a sex-shared interneuron, delayed cholinergic identity in some sex-specific neurons, broad ACh-gated anion-channel expression, and seven transcription factors (six homeobox plus unc-3) controlling identity in 20 cholinergic neuron types.
ocar.future_work: They present the map as a resource for development and function, including further combinatorial transcription-factor logic and the evolutionary hypothesis that ACh is an ancient sensory-motor transmitter.

summaries.beginner: The worm wiring diagram says who touches whom, but not what chemical each cell uses. This study finds that acetylcholine is the most common messenger, maps every cell that uses it in both sexes, and names genes that turn that identity on.
summaries.intermediate: Pereira et al. in eLife (2015) map all cholinergic neurons in male and hermaphrodite C. elegans. ACh is the most broadly used transmitter; a sex-shared interneuron switches from glutamate to ACh in males. ACh-gated anion channels are broadly expressed, implying widespread inhibition. Seven transcription factors, six of them homeobox genes, control cholinergic identity in 20 neuron types.
summaries.advanced: Breadth of ACh use is nematode-specific and contrasted by the authors with vertebrates. Inhibitory ACh is inferred from anion-channel expression patterns, not from a full physiological census. The seven regulators cover 20 types, not every cholinergic neuron. Connectome motif analyses are summarized qualitatively in the selected conclusions.

plain_language_summary: The worm wiring diagram says who touches whom, but not what chemical each cell uses. This study finds that acetylcholine is the most common messenger, maps every cell that uses it in both sexes, and names genes that turn that identity on.
